newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: Difficult road ahead for S.Korean financial reform.
newsitem.headline: Difficult road ahead for S.Korean financial reform.

text.p: South Korea's finance minister pledged on Thursday to submit legislation implementing financial reforms to parliament in August, but analysts said they doubted lawmakers would adopt the controversial measures.

Underscoring the difficulties facing the government, South Korea's main opposition party and central bank employees on Thursday renewed their vows to block parliament's passage of the legislation, first announced on June 16.
They maintained their opposition despite the ministry's announcement on Thursday of revisions to the draft reforms that addressed several of the more controversial clauses.

The ministry eliminated a clause making the central bank's head responsible for meeting annual inflation targets. The revised reforms also would prevent the finance minister from influencing monetary policy.
"I plan to submit the financial reform legislation in early August to the National Assembly based on the revised draft," Finance Minister Kang Kyong-shik told reporters.
"I would like to stress the importance of implementing financial reform as soon as possible to solve structural problems and weakeness of our economy," he said.

However, a controversial provision to establish a single watchdog body to oversee banks, insurers and securities remained unchanged. The new supervisory organisation would be under direct control of the prime minister.

Under the new laws, the Monetary Board would independently set monetary policies, which would be implemented by the Bank of Korea. The bank would govern settlement-linked business and other administrative activities related with monetary policy.
"I believe the revision will clarify the authority and independence of the central bank and improve the effectiveness of the unified supervisory body," Kang said.
The opposition National Congress for New Politics party and central Bank of Korea employees were unmoved.

"It's not satisfactory at all. The supervisory function is one of the key roles the central bank should assume in order to pursue monetary policy effectively," said an official at the central bank's finance rescue committee.
The opposition party agreed in principle on the need to modernise South Korea's backward financial industry.

"Financial reform means letting the institutions do everything they want. But the government is still trying to maintain its control in the industry," said Lee Sang-wook, the party's economic specialist.
"We cannot accept the idea and will oppose the bill in the parliamentary session," he added.
Economists also remained sceptical whether President Kim Young-sam would be able to achieve meaningful economic reform before his term ends in February.
They said lawmakers, concerned about votes, were unlikely to take up contentious issues so near a presidential election.
"The lame-duck government has a very slim chance," said Lee Han-koo, president of Daewoo Economic Research Institute.
Shocked by a loans-for-kickback scandal involving the failed Hanbo Steel Co, South Korea had promised "big bang" style financial reform like Britain's reforms of 1986.
Analysts said they're still waiting for the big bang.
"It's far from a big bang," said Kim Min-tae, economist at LG Economic Research Institute. "If the government really wanted it, they should have pushed foward much earlier."
